USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue negotiations with China while holding existing tariff leverage. The 90-day truce window is active with high-level talks underway (Lighthizer/Mnuchin met Liu He on Jan 30). The US should press hard on structural issues—IP theft, forced tech transfer, state subsidies, enforcement mechanisms—while remaining open to a deal that addresses these core concerns. Do not rush a purchase-only deal before the March 1 deadline; that would squander leverage. The Huawei indictments (Jan 28) reinforce the pressure campaign and signal the US will use law enforcement tools alongside tariffs.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The US position is one of moderate advantage, not crisis. China's economy is under significantly more stress: 2018 GDP slowed to a 28-year low of 6.6%, Q4 at 6.4%, exports contracted in December, factories in Guangdong are closing early, and the CSI 300 fell 26% in 2018 (timeline entry: China retaliated proportionally but its economy is absorbing more damage). Trump himself noted on Jan 21 that China's slowing numbers mean 'it makes sense for China to finally do a Real Deal.' The US has maintained tariff pressure on ~$250B of Chinese goods while the Huawei indictments add a powerful non-tariff lever that China cannot easily counter (NYT, Jan 29: 'neither Huawei nor the Chinese government has easy options for responding'). However, the US is not without cost: the S&P 500 suffered its worst December since 1931, losing ~20% from peak to near-bear territory; 10-year Treasury yields fell from 3.25% to 2.70% signaling growth concerns; business confidence is chilled by supply chain uncertainty; and agricultural constituencies face real pain from Chinese retaliation on soybeans and other goods. The trade war has contributed to $15 trillion in global wealth destruction. These domestic costs argue against further escalation at this moment. The right stance is to negotiate firmly from a position of relative strength—China needs a deal more than we do—while preserving the option to escalate to 25% tariffs on List 3 if structural demands are not met by March 1. A narrow purchase-only deal would fail to address the long-term strategic challenge of China's state-led tech ambitions (Made in China 2025). The USTR statement on Jan 9 emphasized 'complete implementation subject to ongoing verification and effective enforcement'—this should remain the standard.
key_factors: China GDP at 28-year low (6.6% in 2018, 6.4% Q4) — US has asymmetric leverage
US stock market near bear territory (-19.8% from peak) — domestic cost of escalation is real
Huawei indictments (Jan 28) add non-tariff pressure China cannot easily counter
Structural issues (IP, tech transfer, Made in China 2025) unresolved in Jan 7-9 talks
March 1 deadline for 25% tariff hike on List 3 creates urgency
China's retaliatory tariffs hurting US agriculture — domestic political pressure
Lighthizer vs Mnuchin tension: structural reforms vs purchase-only deal

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing for high-level talks. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
Fed funds rate at 2.40% (Jan 2019), up from 1.95% in Sep — tightening cycle ongoing.
10-year Treasury yield fell from 3.25% peak (Oct) to 2.70% (Jan 30) — significant decline signaling growth concerns.
China's 2018 GDP grew 6.6%, slowest since 1990. Q4 at 6.4%, slowest since financial crisis. Exports contracted in December.
Neither Huawei nor the Chinese government has easy options for responding or retaliating. China is in the middle of a trade war it is eager to end as its vast economy slows.

Lighthizer's stance emphasized structural changes and 'complete implementation subject to ongoing verification and effective enforcement.' China's definition of reformable areas excludes precisely the areas of most U.S. concern.
